title: Languages
body:
A language is any subset of $\Sigma^*$: a set of [[Strings]] over an [[Alphabet]]. That is it.
No grammar required, no meaning attached.

Every machine in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] exists to answer one question about one
language: **is this string in it?** The whole course is the discovery that different machines
can answer that for different sets of languages.

- $\emptyset$ (no strings) and $\{\varepsilon\}$ (one string, the empty one) are different
  languages. This distinction shows up on exams.
- $\Sigma^*$ itself is a language.
- Languages are sets, so union, intersection, and complement all mean what [[Sets]] says they
  mean. Concatenation $L_1 L_2$ and Kleene star $L^*$ are the two extra operations.

The classes, smallest first, are the [[Chomsky Hierarchy]]: [[Regular Languages]]
([[Finite Automata]]) ⊂ context-free ([[Pushdown Automata]]) ⊂ context-sensitive ⊂
recursively enumerable ([[Turing Machine]]).
